newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's growth targets could be beaten - Arthuis.
newsitem.headline: France's growth targets could be beaten - Arthuis.

text.p: France's finance minister said on Wednesday the government's growth forecast of 2.3 percent for this year should be considered a "floor" for the economy while its 2.8 percent forecast for 1998 may also be surpassed.
"The 2.3 percent forecast (for 1997) is a floor," Jean Arthuis told a news conference on the government's latest review of its official economic forecasts.
Next year's growth target of 2.8 percent "may even be exceeded" if investment and consumption were more dynamic than expected, he said.

Speaking about the government's targets for 1997, Arthuis said, "We have stayed with a prudent forecast of 2.3 percent growth...My personal feeling is that in the coming months we will observe a progression on this forecast."
He declined to say how high he thought growth could be.
But he said it proved government policies had been right.
"This improvement (in the economy) demonstrates that the economic policy which we have carried out for the past two years is beginning to bear fruit. We must maintain our course."
He reiterated the government would stick to its deficit target this year.
France is targeting a public deficit to GDP ratio of three percent for 1997, in line with the Maastricht Treaty goal for EU economic and monetary union.
Arthuis said the government was forecasting net new job creations of 120,000 to 140,000 in the non-farm market sector this year and 220,000 to 250,000 in 1998.

He declined to say what he expected the unemployment rate, which reached a record 12.8 percent in February, would be at the end of the year. But he saw better news on unemployment arriving from the second half of this year.
"The situation should improve in the second half (of 1997)," he said. In 1998, "we should see unemployment falling".
A government statement earlier said Europe as a whole should enjoy accelerating non-inflationary growth in the next two years.
It said the main downside risk would be if U.S. economic growth failed to slow down as expected, leading to upward pressure on long-term interest rates, both in the U.S. and Europe.
Asked about this, however, Arthuis noted the market had remained calm after the last quarter-point U.S. rate rise in March.
"There is nothing of a nature to threaten our forecasts," he said.
